title: SUPPORT for Patients and Communities Reauthorization Act of 2025
official_title: To reauthorize certain programs that provide for opioid use disorder prevention, treatment, and recovery, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-44. Passed the House June 4, 2025 and the Senate September 18, 2025, and was signed into law December 1, 2025. A reauthorization of existing opioid programs originally created by the bipartisan 2018 SUPPORT Act.
summary: Reauthorizes the opioid prevention, treatment, and recovery programs created by the 2018 SUPPORT Act through fiscal year 2030, mostly at higher funding levels, and adds new provisions covering fetal alcohol spectrum disorder services, cybersecurity for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, fentanyl-contamination coordination, at-home drug disposal, and expanded prescriber training.
brief: Reauthorizes the 2018 SUPPORT Act's opioid programs through 2030 at higher funding, plus new FASD, 988 cybersecurity, and fentanyl provisions.

top_lines.headline: Reauthorizes the Opioid Response Through 2030
subs: Extends dozens of prevention, treatment, and recovery programs from the 2018 SUPPORT Act through fiscal year 2030
Most reauthorized programs get funding increases (e.g., overdose prevention rises to $505.58M/year; first-responder training $36M to $57M/year)
Allows fentanyl and xylazine test strips under State and Tribal opioid response grants

top_lines.headline: New and Expanded Health Programs
subs: Creates a standalone Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder program with $12.5M/year through 2030
Adds cybersecurity reporting requirements for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline plus a GAO study
Raises authorizations for recovery, trauma, and treatment-workforce programs (e.g., Building Communities of Recovery $5M to $17M/year)

top_lines.headline: Fentanyl, Disposal, and Prescriber Provisions
subs: "Bruce's Law" sets up a federal interagency work group on fentanyl contamination of illegal drugs
Directs HHS guidance on at-home drug disposal systems within one year
Expands the list of organizations whose courses satisfy controlled-substance prescriber training

sections.label: Section 103 — Preventing Overdoses of Controlled Substances

items.main: Broadens the CDC overdose-prevention program beyond opioids and reauthorizes it at a higher level.
items.detail: Amends section 392A of the Public Health Service Act so the surveillance and rapid-response grant program covers "substances causing overdose" and associated risk factors rather than opioids alone, and explicitly allows innovative approaches such as wastewater surveillance. The authorization rises from $496M to $505.58M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030.

sections.label: Section 104 — Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder Program

items.main: Replaces the existing FASD provisions with a new prevention, intervention, and services program.
items.detail: Rewrites Part O of title III of the Public Health Service Act to establish an FASD education, prevention, identification, intervention, and services-delivery program, with grants and technical assistance to states, Tribes, local governments, and nonprofits, and a separate capacity-building and clearinghouse role. It authorizes $12.5M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030 and requires HHS to report to Congress within four years and annually thereafter.

items.main: Expands the first-responder overdose training program beyond opioids and increases its funding.
items.detail: Amends section 546 of the Public Health Service Act to cover overdose-reversal drugs that are "approved, cleared, or otherwise legally marketed" and to address heroin and other drug overdoses, not just opioids. The authorization rises from $36M to $57M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030.

sections.label: Section 107 — Donald J. Cohen National Child Traumatic Stress Initiative

items.main: Reauthorizes the National Child Traumatic Stress Initiative and adds a dissemination role for grantees.
items.detail: Amends section 582 of the Public Health Service Act to require NCTSI grantees to develop trainings and resources that support implementation of the evidence-based practices they develop. It authorizes $98.89M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2028 and $100M for each of fiscal years 2029 and 2030.

sections.label: Section 108 — Protecting the 988 Lifeline From Cybersecurity Incidents

items.main: Adds cybersecurity protection and reporting requirements for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.
items.detail: Amends section 520E-3 of the Public Health Service Act to require the Lifeline program to take steps to protect against cybersecurity incidents and eliminate known vulnerabilities, and to require the program's network administrator and participating crisis centers to report identified vulnerabilities and incidents to the Assistant Secretary in a privacy-protective manner. It also directs the Comptroller General to complete a study of cybersecurity risks to the 988 Lifeline within 180 days of enactment.

items.main: Strengthens youth fentanyl-awareness work and creates a federal work group on fentanyl-contaminated illegal drugs.
items.detail: Amends the youth prevention provisions of the 2018 SUPPORT Act to add education on the potency and dangers of synthetic opioids, including drugs contaminated with fentanyl. It directs the Interdepartmental Substance Use Disorders Coordinating Committee to establish a Federal Interagency Work Group on Fentanyl Contamination of Illegal Drugs, which consults with families of overdose victims and reports annually with recommendations. The Coordinating Committee is set to terminate September 30, 2030.

sections.label: Section 113 — State and Tribal Opioid Response Grants

items.main: Allows opioid response grant funds to be used for drug-detection tools such as fentanyl and xylazine test strips.
items.detail: Clarifies that activities under the 21st Century Cures Act State and Tribal opioid response grant program may include facilitating access to products that detect substances such as fentanyl and xylazine test strips, to the extent their purchase and possession is consistent with federal and state law.

sections.label: Section 204 — Loan Repayment for the Treatment Workforce

items.main: Reauthorizes the substance use disorder treatment workforce loan-repayment program at a higher level.
items.detail: Amends section 781 of the Public Health Service Act, raising the authorization from $25M to $40M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030.

items.main: Directs HHS to review the controlled-substance scheduling of approved buprenorphine-naloxone combination products.
items.detail: Requires the Secretary of HHS to review data on the scheduling of FDA-approved products containing a combination of buprenorphine and naloxone and, if appropriate, ask the Attorney General to begin rulemaking to revise the schedules. The Attorney General must review any such request under the Controlled Substances Act criteria.

items.main: Sharply increases funding for the Building Communities of Recovery program.
items.detail: Amends section 547 of the Public Health Service Act, raising the authorization from $5M to $17M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030.

items.main: Reauthorizes and expands the youth prevention and recovery program with a rising funding schedule.
items.detail: Amends section 7102(c) of the 2018 SUPPORT Act to broaden eligible applicants (including consortia of local educational agencies and secondary schools) and require sustainability plans. It authorizes $10M for fiscal year 2026, $12M for 2027, $13M for 2028, $14M for 2029, and $15M for 2030.

items.main: Reauthorizes the CAREER Act workforce grants and the recovery housing pilot, with new performance reporting.
items.detail: Amends section 7183 of the 2018 SUPPORT Act to rename the program, update the targeting formula to use 2018-2022 overdose, unemployment, and labor-force data, allow up to 5 percent of grant funds for transportation, and add employment-and-earnings outcome reporting. It raises the authorization from $5M to $12M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030 and reauthorizes the recovery housing pilot program through 2030.

sections.label: Section 401 — Pharmacy Delivery to a Prescribing Practitioner

items.main: Adjusts when a pharmacy may deliver a controlled substance to a prescribing practitioner for administration.
items.detail: Amends section 309A of the Controlled Substances Act so the exception covers schedule III, IV, or V drugs administered by injection or implantation for maintenance or detoxification treatment, or drugs subject to an FDA risk evaluation and mitigation strategy that includes post-administration monitoring by a health care provider.

items.main: Expands the list of organizations and schools whose courses satisfy controlled-substance prescriber training.
items.detail: Amends section 303 of the Controlled Substances Act to add organizations such as the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American Podiatric Medical Association, the Academy of General Dentistry, the American Optometric Association, the American Pharmacists Association, and others, and to include podiatric medicine and accredited schools of pharmacy. The amendment takes effect as if enacted on December 29, 2022.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Latta
featured_quotes.text: I appreciate it. The SUPPORT for Patients and Communities Reauthorization Act of 2025 is one of the most impactful bills the Committee on Energy and Commerce has worked on during my time in Congress. Simply put, we came together to implement bipartisan policies that would save lives. Gone are the days that substance abuse and addiction are a far off problem that doesn't impact each one of our districts.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Dunn
featured_quotes.text: This bill is a critical piece of legislation that will help bolster prevention, treatment, and recovery for millions of Americans suffering from substance abuse disorders. Thanks to the investments from the original SUPPORT for Patients and Communities Act in 2018 and the efforts of the Trump administration, we are finally starting to see a decrease in the overdose death rate. Florida is a shining example of this progress.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Dexter
featured_quotes.text: I rise today not just as a Member of this body but as a physician who has spent nearly two decades caring for patients in the intensive care unit, many of them fighting for their lives because of a system that has failed to support them before a crisis hit. In Oregon's Third District, we see every day how critical prevention, treatment, and recovery programs are. We need those programs that my colleague from New Jersey just referred to as being cut. This bill does nothing to repair those cuts. These aren't abstract policy ideas.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Hassan
featured_quotes.text: I rise today to pass into law a lifesaving bipartisan legislation that will enable us to keep fighting the opioid and fentanyl epidemic, an epidemic that has destroyed families and devastated communities all across our country. Our country faces many challenges, and I am sure we will continue to debate in the coming weeks how to address those, but today we will advance, on a bipartisan basis, lifesaving legislation that we know is working to combat fentanyl.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Cassidy
featured_quotes.text: It is part of, as a doctor, I would say, a pro-patient--we would say pro-family--agenda that we wish to deliver for the American people. About a month and a half ago, President Trump had a signing ceremony for the HALT Fentanyl Act at the White House. That was my bill, so I was privileged to be there. Behind him were families holding the pictures of their children who had died from fentanyl overdose. Incredibly moving. I had a similar ceremony in Baton Rouge where, across Louisiana, people came and held a picture of their child who had died.

added: New Sec. 210 — HHS must make any reference to an opioid overdose reversal drug (such as naloxone) in grant-program regulations/guidance inclusive of any FDA-approved reversal drug; existing references updated within one year

New Sec. 211 — National Coordinator for Health IT must convene a public roundtable within 180 days on using electronic health records to improve mental health and substance use care outcomes, then report
New Sec. 307 — HHS must convene a public meeting within one year to improve awareness of and access to SAMHSA funding opportunities, improve Grants.gov, and report
